passage:
Chinmay hadn't seen his sister Jasleen in six months, though her in-laws' house was only two bus stops past the mandi.
She opened the door smiling too brightly. Her husband, Gurmeet, sat on the charpai with her phone in his hand.
Over tea, Chinmay noticed things. Jasleen glanced at Gurmeet before answering even simple questions. She said she had given up her tailoring work for the house. When Chinmay mentioned Bebe's birthday next week, Gurmeet said, "We'll see," and Jasleen said nothing.
At the gate, alone for a minute, Chinmay didn't say leave him, or why do you put up with this. He knew pushing could drive her further in.
He said, "I'll call every Sunday at eleven. If you don't pick up, I'll just call again. Bebe and I are always there. Any time."
Jasleen squeezed his hand hard, once, and went inside.

qa.q: How far was Jasleen's in-laws' house?
qa.a: It was only two bus stops past the mandi.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's glance at Gurmeet before answering suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels watched and anxious, checking whether each answer is allowed.

qa.q: Why was Chinmay's promise at the gate a wise choice?
qa.a: Instead of blaming or pushing her to leave, he set a steady Sunday call and said he and Bebe are always there, keeping a safe line open.

qa.q: What might Jasleen's hard squeeze of his hand mean?
qa.a: It may mean gratitude and a silent sign that something is wrong, even though she cannot say it out loud there.

grounding: A brother visiting his sister notices her anxious glances, lost work and a husband holding her phone, and keeps in touch without blame rather than pushing her to leave.

passage:
Liam and Bao had shared a flat in Dublin for three years before Bao moved in with his girlfriend. Now Liam saw him once a month, if that.
Each time, Liam noticed more. Bao checked his phone every few minutes and texted where he was: "at the pub with Liam," "leaving now," "on the bus." When Liam offered to split the bill, Bao said quietly, "I don't have my card. She keeps it now. It's easier."
He used to laugh loudly. Now he looked at the door a lot.
Liam wanted to say, "Mate, this is not right. Leave." But he'd read that pushing too hard can drive someone back, closer to the person controlling them.
So he said, "I miss you. I'm always around. Pub every second Friday? My treat until you sort the card thing." And, before Bao left: "If you ever need anything, day or night, call me."
Bao nodded, and held on a second too long in the hug.

qa.q: Who keeps Bao's card now?
qa.a: She keeps it now.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling as he noticed the changes in Bao?
qa.a: Liam felt worried and frustrated, wanting to tell Bao to leave but holding back so as not to push him away.

qa.q: What did Liam do that fits a helpful response?
qa.a: He stayed in touch without blame, offered regular meetups and made clear Bao could call him any time.

qa.q: How does Bao seem to feel during the meetup?
qa.a: Bao seems anxious and watchful, checking his phone and the door, and grateful, holding the hug a second too long.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing someone becoming isolated, anxious, reporting his whereabouts and losing his money, and staying in touch without blame.

passage:
In the small clinic where they both worked as receptionists, Arohi had started noticing things about Tenzin.
She used to come to the staff lunch every Friday. Now she ate alone at her desk, and when Arohi asked, she said she'd forgotten her money again. Her husband handled everything, she said. She texted him before she went to the pharmacy next door, and after she came back. Her phone buzzed whenever she was two minutes late.
Arohi's first impulse was to say, "Tenzin, this isn't normal. You should leave him." She didn't. She'd seen a cousin pushed that way once, and the cousin had cut everyone off.
Instead, on Friday, she brought two tiffins. "I made too much. Eat with me?" They talked about nothing. Before Tenzin went back to her desk, Arohi said, "Whatever you need, anytime, I'm here. No questions."
Tenzin's eyes filled. She nodded, and took the tiffin box back with her.

qa.q: Who does Tenzin text before going to the pharmacy?
qa.a: She texted her husband.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she first noticed the signs?
qa.a: Arohi felt worried and alarmed, with an urge to tell Tenzin to leave, which she held back.

qa.q: Why did Arohi avoid pushing Tenzin to leave?
qa.a: She had seen a cousin cut everyone off after being pushed, so she chose to stay close and offer support without blame.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when Arohi offered help with no questions?
qa.a: Tenzin felt moved and grateful, her eyes filling as she nodded.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing isolation, anxiety, constant check-ins and lost access to money, and staying close without blame.

passage:
Dear Lavanya,
I've been thinking about Diwali all week.
You looked so tired. You checked your phone every few minutes and texted Rohit where you were, even when you went to the kitchen. When Ma asked you to come shopping, you said you didn't have money with you, though you've always earned more than me. You didn't laugh once.
I want to say something, and then I promise I won't push.
I'm not asking you to leave anyone. I'm not judging you. I'm just here. You can call me at any time, even at 2 a.m., and I will come. You can tell me anything, or nothing. I've also saved a helpline number and I can give it to you if you ever want it.
Whatever you decide, I'm your sister first. Always.
Next Sunday I'm making rajma. Come if you can. If you can't, I'll call you.
Yamini

qa.q: What was Yamini making next Sunday?
qa.a: Next Sunday Yamini is making rajma.

qa.q: What is Yamini feeling while writing?
qa.a: Yamini feels worried and protective, having noticed Lavanya's tiredness and constant check-ins at Diwali.

qa.q: How does Yamini try to help without pushing?
qa.a: Yamini promises not to judge or ask Lavanya to leave, offers to come anytime, mentions a helpline number if wanted, and invites Lavanya for rajma.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lavanya might feel relieved and less alone, knowing Yamini will stay close whatever Lavanya decides.

grounding: A sister writes to her sibling after noticing isolation, anxiety and lost money, staying in touch without blame or pressure.

passage: People ask what we noticed first, as Seema's family. Honestly, small things. My sister used to call Ammi every evening; then it became Sundays, then only when her husband was home, on speaker. At Eid she kept sending him photos: "I'm at Ammi's, see." She said she had no money for gifts, and Seema has earned her own salary since she was twenty-two. My first instinct was to storm over and say, "Pack your bags, you're coming home." Our aunt did exactly that, and Seema didn't speak to her for three months. So I, Irfan, the loud brother, learned to be quiet. I message her about silly things, cricket, recipes. I never say his name with anger. Once I told her, "Whatever happens, my door is open, no questions." Last week, for the first time, she asked if we could meet at the library, just the two of us.

qa.q: How did Seema's calls to Ammi change?
qa.a: From every evening to Sundays, then only when her husband was home, on speaker.

qa.q: What was Irfan's first instinct, and why did he hold back?
qa.a: Irfan felt angry and protective and wanted to storm over, but held back after seeing Seema stop speaking to their aunt for three months.

qa.q: What could Irfan do if Seema opens up at the library?
qa.a: Listen without blame, let Seema lead, and offer to help her reach a helpline or support service when she's ready, so any step is planned safely.

qa.q: Why might Seema have cut off the aunt who told her to pack her bags?
qa.a: Pressure to leave may have made Seema feel judged and cornered, pushing her away from the family and further into isolation.
